      Better public procurement for IT in India
      Working paper · Ashok Pal Singh, Karthik Suresh, Susan Thomas · XKDR Forum Working Paper 51 · Oct 2026
      Public procurementTechnology and innovation
      LEAP blog post
      AbstractInformation technology (IT) systems are now ubiquitous in government. The Government of India has tripled its spending in real terms on IT procurement over the last fifteen years. IT procurement is tricky because these systems need continuous maintenance and refinement, and traditional systems of procurement are unsuitable for solving the incomplete contract problem that follows IT procurement. We build on three case studies from India – Aadhaar, Passport Seva, and MCA-21 – to make the case for why we need new thinking on IT procurement. Our solutions hinge around the fact that the government needs to build robust internal technical expertise even when system development has been outsourced. We make the case for flexible contracting, early concept verification, and strategic investments in state HR capabilities to successfully navigate the marketplace for digital services.

      Better methods of running subsidy programs: Evidence from the Karnataka schemes of 2023
      Working paper · Jay Kulkarni, Ajay Shah, Susan Thomas · XKDR Forum Working Paper 50 · Aug 2026
      Households and inclusionPublic financeMeasurement and data
      
      AbstractGovernments in developing countries spend heavily on subsidies, yet much of the money never reaches households: the macro–micro gap. We measure this gap in Karnataka, India, across a natural experiment. Karnataka has been delivering conditional Direct Benefit Transfers (DBT) for about a decade now. In July 2023 the state introduced new “guarantee” schemes, and directed much of its DBT allocation to a near-unconditional scheme. Because administrative records are endogenous to the state that produces them, we measure household receipts independently, from the CMIE Consumer Pyramids Household Survey. We compare robust population estimates from this survey against the state’s reported expenditure on DBTs in both periods. The gap averaged about 78% over the seven pre-2023 years and fell to about 17% after the shift. The paper contributes independently measured evidence on subsidy delivery in India and a replicable method for auditing welfare programs in the presence of longitudinal data.
    
  

  
    
    
      When households first borrow: Causes and consequences
      Working paper · Geetika Palta, Renuka Sane, Susan Thomas · XKDR Forum Working Paper 49 · Jun 2026
      Financial marketsBanking and creditHouseholds and inclusionPublic finance
      
      AbstractWe examine the impact of borrowing on consumption smoothing for households entering credit markets for the first time, using a large panel dataset with income, expenditure and financial choices of 150,000 households in India. Compared to households that never borrow, first-time borrowers are poorer, younger, less educated, and face higher income volatility. Their decision to borrow is often preceded by a change in income or consumption, regardless of whether it is a decrease or an increase. The act of borrowing increases both the level and the volatility of consumption expenditure. Credit does not help to smooth consumption, even for first time borrowers with no shocks to income and consumption. Higher volatility of consumption persists after borrowing, particularly for expenditure on non-durable goods such as food or planned household expenditure. This suggests that new borrowers use credit as one component of a broader risk-management strategy that involves multiple adjustments within their consumption portfolio.

      Measurement and impact assessment of Karnataka's 2023 guarantee schemes
      Journal article · Sanjuktha B. Athreya, Utkarsh Narain, Geetika Palta, Susan Thomas · Aarthika Charche 10(2), 42–51 · Dec 2025
      Households and inclusionPublic financeMeasurement and data
      
      AbstractThe proliferation of large-scale conditional and unconditional cash transfers in emerging economies necessitates novel measurement frameworks that move eyond administrative delivery tracking to capture complex socio-economic impacts. In July 2023, the Government of Karnataka implemented five major ‘guarantee schemes’ designed to alleviate poverty through cash transfers and targeted utility subsidies. This paper establishes an evaluation framework to assess these schemes, shifting the analytical lens toward household welfare, labour market dynamics, and macroeconomic opportunity costs. We use a high-frequency monthly panel dataset of approximately 6,000 households in Karnataka, contrasted against a control group of 12,000 households from bordering states (January 2022 to December 2024) to measure both direct consumption smoothing, and structural economic shifts. While the data indicates successful, large-scale consumption smoothing, we find negligible improvements in structural indicators, such as women’s intra-household agency and female Labour Force articipation Rates. We argue that comprehensive scheme evaluation must prioritise structural and macroeconomic indicators to prevent welfare programs from inadvertently substituting necessary, long-term economic growth strategies.
    
  

  
    
    
      Information extraction from fiscal documents using LLMs
      Working paper · Vikram Aggarwal, Jay Kulkarni, Aditi Mascarenhas, Aakriti Narang, Siddarth Raman, Ajay Shah, Susan Thomas · XKDR Forum Working Paper 43 · Nov 2025
      Public financeMeasurement and dataTechnology and innovation
      
      AbstractLarge Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in text comprehension, but their ability to process complex, hierarchical tabular data remains underexplored. We present a novel approach to extracting structured data from multi-page government fiscal documents using LLM-based techniques. Applied to large annual fiscal documents from the State of Karnataka in India, our method achieves high accuracy through a multi-stage pipeline that leverages domain knowledge, sequential context, and algorithmic validation. Traditional OCR methods work poorly with errors that are hard to detect. The inherent structure of fiscal tables, with totals at each level of the hierarchy, allows for robust internal validation of the extracted data. We use these hierarchical relationships to create multi-level validation checks. We demonstrate that LLMs can read tables and also process document-specific structural hierarchies, offering a scalable process for converting PDF-based fiscal disclosures into research-ready databases. Our implementation shows promise for broader applications across developing country contexts.

      Shedding light on the Russia-Ukraine war
      Working paper · Rounak Hande, Ayush Patnaik, Ajay Shah, Susan Thomas · XKDR Forum Working Paper 40 · Aug 2025
      Measurement and data
      LEAP blog post
      AbstractWith the Russia–Ukraine war evolving into a prolonged war of attrition, the functioning of the two economies has become central. A small but growing literature uses alternative data to measure economic activity, responding to the limitations of official statistics. In this paper, we use nighttime lights (“NTL”) data to track economic changes in both countries. Ukraine’s NTL has fallen by 50% compared to 2022 levels. In contrast, Russia’s aggregate NTL showed virtually no change between 2022 and 2025. Within Russia, the Yamal–Nenets Autonomous Okrug, which produces 90% of the country’s gas, recorded substantial ntl growth despite reports of declining national gas production. We also identify growth reversals in regions hundreds of kilometres from the Ukrainian border, likely reflecting the effects of standoff weapons. Similar reversals appear along Russia’s Western European border but not along other international frontiers, suggesting uneven enforcement of sanctions. Over the war years, Ukraine’s economic activity has shifted westward, while Russia’s has moved eastward.

      Incremental reform of banking law in India
      Working paper · K. P. Krishnan, Ajay Shah, Susan Thomas, Diya Uday, Harsh Vardhan · XKDR Forum Working Paper 39 · May 2025
      Banking and creditLaw and regulation
      
      AbstractA banking sector regulator must be non-partisan and separate from government. However, the banking sector in India comprises banks of many kinds: private banks, public sector banks, cooperative banks, and regional rural banks. The laws that govern the sector have evolved to grant special powers over some categories of banks to the Union government, thereby, diluting or sometimes even nullifying the power of the Indian banking regulator, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), over these banks. In most cases, the power of the RBI has been diluted or nullified in respect of public sector banks and the State Bank of India. This is not desirable from the perspective of ownership neutral regulation and creates an unfair playing field for banks in the sector. It also raises serious conflict of interest concerns, where the government is both a borrower and regulator, can influence the functioning of some banks. This article examines the legal provisions that undermine the regulatory powers of the RBI including on shareholding, appointment of directors, winding up and making schemes. It argues for an ownership-neutral regulatory framework emphasising the need for greater autonomy for the RBI, and the creation of a clear separation between the governments borrowing and regulatory role. The aim is to chart the pathway towards a more robust regulation of the banking sector in India.

      Rethinking innovation policy in India: Amplifying spillovers through contracting-out
      Journal article · R. A. Mashelkar, Ajay Shah, Susan Thomas · Accounting Theory and Practice 1 · Dec 2024
      Public procurementTechnology and innovation
      LEAP blog postWorking paper
      AbstractAt independence, India committed itself fully to foster, promote and sustain the creation of science and scientific research in all aspects. In this paper, we present first principles reasoning on the case for state action, and the optimal mechanisms for using taxpayer resources, to fulfill this commitment. We argue in favour of a reorientation of public spending on innovation: away from building vertical government organisations, and in favour of a contracting-out strategy. Such a strategy would induce knowledge and capabilities in the society, and through this, induce greater gains for the people of India. We present a preliminary sketch of the path to implementation.
    
  

  
    
    
      Improving supply chain management of medicines for public healthcare in India
      Working paper · Pavithra Manivannan, Charmi Mehta, Susan Thomas · XKDR Forum Working paper 36 · Dec 2024
      Public procurementFinancial markets
      
      AbstractThis paper examines the prerequisites for successful drug procurement within the Indian public healthcare system. It argues that the primal objective is timely availability of medicines, and analyses two successful procurement cases, from which four common elements emerge. One, an information system on stocks and flows of medicine. Two, processes and manuals covering the full pipeline of the procurement contract. Three, procedures and work allocation during emergencies. Four, an information system on present and prospective vendors. These elements, coupled with a supply-chain focused mandate on delivery to the end user, and investments in regular training of personnel, enable a public healthcare system that can deliver medicines reliably.
    
  

  
    
    
      Who lends to the Indian state?
      Working paper · Aneesha Chitgupi, Ajay Shah, Manish K. Singh, Susan Thomas, Harsh Vardhan · XKDR Forum Working paper 34 · Aug 2024
      Banking and creditHouseholds and inclusionPublic financeLaw and regulation
      LEAP blog post
      AbstractMuch of Indian public finance research has focused on the level of debt and deficits. In this paper, we examine the structure of lenders to the Indian state. To what extent is this lending coerced? Is the present debt management strategy consistent with the objectives of low cost borrowing for the government in the long run, while preserving efficiency in the economy, and retaining the optionality of surging borrowing when faced with rare events? We find 5% of the lending to the Indian state comes from voluntary sources. While financial repression for banks eased de jure with a decline in the SLR from 33% in 1988 to 18% in 2021, lending to the state beyond regulatory requirements was Rs.30 trillion in 2021. Alongside this, the growth of the pension and insurance industries created new pools of assets where financial repression generated bountiful lending to the government. These facts help re-examine debt management strategy in India.

      Do decreases in Distance-to-Default predict rating downgrades?
      Journal article · Nidhi Aggarwal, Manish Singh, Susan Thomas · Economic Modelling 129 · Dec 2023
      Banking and creditMeasurement and dataLaw and regulation
      Working paper
      AbstractCredit rating agencies have long been criticized for being slow to downgrade ratings, when the financial health of the firm deteriorates. This stands out in sharp contrast to how security market prices of the firm respond more rapidly, during the same time. In this paper, we ask whether this disparity between the two indicators can be bridged. We estimate a logit model for the probability of a rating downgrade, using a large dataset of firms in India which combines both high frequency market price data and lower frequency accounting data. We find that changes in measures such as the Distance to Default, in combination with firm characteristics such as ownership structure, can predict a higher probability of ratings downgrades, before they are announced. This will be particularly useful for regulated financial firms, which have to re-weight their portfolios to satisfy micro-prudential requirements, based on downgrades in credit ratings.
    
  

  
    
    
      Evaluating courts from a litigant's perspective: A project report
      Working paper · Pavithra Manivannan, Geetika Palta, Susan Thomas, Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah · XKDR Forum · Dec 2023
      Courts and insolvencyMeasurement and data
      
      AbstractInformation systems about dispute resolution processes and forums that can aid litigants, a key stakeholder in the justice delivery system, are absent. We propose the development of a system that allows a litigant to comparatively evaluate the different forums where he can take his dispute for resolution. To develop this system, we first identify the types of information that can support the decision of a potential litigant on whether to take her matter to court and if yes, which court. We find that information on efficiency, effectiveness, fairness, predictability, and access to courts are crucial for a litigant's decision-making process. Subsequently, we locate data sources required to quantify such measures from the viewpoint of periodically publishing such measures in the public domain. For this purpose, the case type was narrowed down to debt disputes. We systematically collect quantifiable information about cases from the select courts' websites, namely, the Bombay High Court (Bombay HC), the Mumbai bench of the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), and the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT). We use data from these courts up to September 2022. We find that a litigant has the lowest chance of getting a first hearing within the first year of filing a case at the Bombay HC (37%) as compared to the NCLT or the DRT. The chance for disposal within the first year is even slimmer. There is a 1/3rd chance of disposal at the NCLT within one year of filing, while it is less than 1/5th at both the Bombay HC and the DRT. However, a case is likely to have the highest number of hearings at the NCLT. A survey questionnaire is designed and deployed to capture features of a case that cannot be quantified. We deploy the survey to capture the relative performance of each of the three courts to a sample of respondents who have litigated frequently in the courts of our interest. The results of the survey indicate that the NCLT is ranked the highest by survey participants. Bombay HC comes second, and the DRT is ranked third.

      Learning by doing for public procurement
      Working paper · Aneesha Chitgupi, Susan Thomas · XKDR Forum Working paper 22 · Sep 2023
      Public procurementPublic financeMeasurement and dataClimate and energy
      LEAP blog post
      AbstractA central choice in public administration is whether to ‘make’, which is production within the public sector, or ‘buy’, which is public procurement. While ‘buy’ has the advantage of harnessing the energy of private firms, it requires state capacity in contracting and leads to questions on how to obtain state capacity in contracting. One measure of state capacity in procurement is the extent of failure to spend resources budgeted for procurement. We construct a novel dataset about spending gaps (between what is budgeted and what is spent) in procurement by the Indian union government. We find that the spending gaps are the smallest when buying goods, and the highest with works. We find that ministries that have a sustained engagement with procurement fare better on obtaining minimum gaps in procurement spending, which suggests a process of learning by doing.

      Measuring Financial Inclusion: A project report
      Working paper · Natasha D'cruze, Indradeep Ghosh, Geetika Palta, Misha Sharma, Susan Thomas · Dvara Research Foundation and XKDR Forum · Feb 2023
      Households and inclusionMeasurement and data
      
      AbstractDespite significant policy support for financial inclusion, there is little evidence about what has been achieved by way of knowing which households and individuals are financially included, or what is the impact of such inclusion on these persons. We propose a measurement framework that aims to capture these aspects of financial inclusion using an input-output-outcome perspective. The input to financial inclusion is measured as participation in formal financial sector instruments. The output is the extent to which these are used. The outcome is how those who hold and use these instruments perceive their own well-being. A survey questionnaire is designed to collect this information, with two distinct features: It is conducted for a household, since financial holdings benefit more than one individual in a household. It is designed to facilitate regular collection, in order to aid financial service providers and policy makers in their thinking about improving financial inclusion. We deploy the questionnaire to understand the financial inclusion of a sample of 300 low-income households in two geographic areas in India. We find that financial participation has a positive correlation with financial well-being, a relationship which is significant even after controlling for income level and ownership of physical assets.

      When is the Order to Trade Ratio fee effective?
      Journal article · Nidhi Aggarwal, Venkatesh Panchapagesan, Susan Thomas · Journal of Financial Markets 62 · Jan 2023
      Financial marketsMeasurement and dataLaw and regulation
      
      AbstractRegulators use measures such as a fee on high order-to-trade ratio (OTR) to slow down high-frequency trading. Their impact on market quality is, however, mixed. We study a natural experiment in the Indian stock market where such a fee was introduced twice, with differences in motivation and implementation. Using a difference-in-difference approach, we find that the fee decreased OTR and improved market quality when it was imposed on all orders, while it had little effect when it was imposed selectively on some orders. Improvement in liquidity was driven by a reduction in adverse selection costs following lower OTR.

      Evaluating contract enforcement by courts in India: a litigant's lens
      Working paper · Pavithra Manivannan, Susan Thomas, Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah · XKDR Forum Working Paper No. 16 · Nov 2022
      Courts and insolvency
      
      AbstractThe literature on the performance evaluation of the judiciary captures the perspectives of judges, researchers and court administrators. However, it is not obvious if a litigant who proposes to access the judiciary for the resolution of a dispute would use the same or similar metrics when evaluating the performance of courts. In this paper, we review the global literature that evaluates the performance of the judiciary and identify which of the metrics in the literature would directly matter to a litigant who proposes to access the courts for redress. Using the litigant’s expectations as performance metrics, we develop an evaluative framework for comparing similar courts. Our work creates the foundation for developing an information system that could potentially help litigants make informed choices when approaching courts.

      But clouds got in my way: Bias and bias correction of VIIRS nighttime lights data in the presence of clouds
      Working paper · Ayush Patnaik, Ajay Shah, Anshul Tayal, Susan Thomas · XKDR Forum Working Paper No. 7 · Oct 2021
      Households and inclusionMeasurement and data
      LEAP blog post
      AbstractThe VIIRS nighttime lights dataset constitutes progress in the measurement of night lights radiance, with monthly data at a pixel of roughly 0.5km ¡Á 0.5km. We identify a downward bias in the reported radiance when the number of cloud-free images in a month is low. This bias often takes on large values from -10% to -30%. We develop a cautious bias-correction scheme which partially addresses this problem. This scheme is applied upon the pixel-level dataset to create an improved dataset. The bias-corrected data hews closer to the ground truth as seen in household survey data.

      From participation to repurchase: Low income households and micro-insurance
      Journal article · Renuka Sane, Susan Thomas · Journal of Risk & Insurance 87(3), 783-814 · Sep 2020
      Households and inclusion
      
      AbstractThe article asks what drives the time to repurchase for life and accident insurance contracts in low income households. We use data on customers of a financial services provider from three states in India and find that the probability of repurchase is highest in the first 2 months after the contract expires, and steadily declines after. This suggests a window of opportunity for financial firms and governments to target customers to ensure continuous insurance purchase. Nonmembership of microfinance groups and poor rainfall in the month of expiry affect the time to repurchase adversely. Customers who take longer to repurchase tend to increase the amount of insurance cover.

      When stock futures dominate price discovery
      Journal article · Nidhi Aggarwal, Susan Thomas · Journal of Futures Markets 39(3), 263-278 · Mar 2019
      Financial markets
      
      AbstractThis paper revisits the role of leverage in price discovery, using one of the most liquid single-stock futures (SSFs) markets in the world. Price discovery is analysed as a dynamic intraday process. We find that the information share of the SSFs is 55% during news arrivals. It increases to 61%, when the news is negative and the futures is preferred because of short-sales restrictions on the spot. A partial equilibrium analysis predicts that the trade-off between leverage and market liquidity determines price discovery across securities. These predictions are validated by empirical evidence.

      The real cost of credit constraints: Evidence from micro-finance
      Journal article · Renuka Sane, Susan Thomas · B E Journal of Applied Economic Analysis and Policy 16(1), 151-183 · Jan 2016
      Banking and creditHouseholds and inclusion
      
      AbstractThe paper studies the effect of a law that banned micro-credit lending in the state of Andhra Pradesh in India. Regions in Andhra Pradesh are matched to regions that did not face the ban. A difference-in-difference estimation of changes in matched regions is used to establish a causal impact on average household consumption in the region. The results show that the average household consumption in the ban-affected regions dropped by 15% immediately after the ban compared to the matched regions, and persisted for four quarters. The result is robust to cross-sectional variations in regional exposure to micro-finance prior to the ban, variation in rural and urban locations and variations in matching strategy. The analysis points to a ban as a sub-optimal intervention to improve customer welfare.

      In search of inclusion: informal sector participation in a voluntary, defined contribution pensions
      Journal article · Renuka Sane, Susan Thomas · Journal of Development Studies 51, 1409-1424 · Aug 2015
      Households and inclusion
      
      AbstractThis paper examines who contributes and who persists in contributing in a national, voluntary, defined contributory pension programme, where the government provides the incentive of matching contributions of a minimum amount (USD 16). The paper uses proprietary data from a financial services firm where 12 per cent of customers (37,000 individuals) chose to participate in this programme. The evidence shows that only about 50 per cent of contributors reach the minimum amount for the co-contribution, but that participants persist in contributing even if they failed to contribute the minimum amount in a given year. While this paper does not provide causal estimates, it does present evidence of considerable interest among the informal sector in a state-run voluntary pension programme in an emerging market where access to formal finance is otherwise poor.

      Journal article · Monika Halan, Renuka Sane, Susan Thomas · Journal of Economic Policy Reform 17, 285-302 · Oct 2014
      Households and inclusionMeasurement and dataLaw and regulation

title: The Long Divergence
text:
(The final calendar entry for the 29 July reading:)
On 29th June, we wrapped up discussing “The long divergence” by Timur Kuran. The book’s strength lies in what it promises: why did the middle eastern countries develop slowly compared to their western counterparts, despite being richer in the 13th century. The book presents a lot of research to answer this, but really struggles with finding a plausible answer. It also struggles with finding it’s identity. Is it a historical narrative? Is it an economic narrative, seeking to establish a causal story? Perhaps an interested reader should just read the last part (Conclusion). It has a summary of the features of Islamic law+the cultural preferences of the people of the Middle East that were in place at the start of the 13th century, and a summary of the three (BIG) features that Kuran is persuaded created the long divergence. But since all this was true for other regions, which didn’t end up in the same place as the Islamic countries, the puzzle is left unresolved. The book has a hopeful end about the Middle East though: that many of the features of the Middle Eastern countries/society that has been attributed to the growth gap are being replaced and adopted integrally with modern institutions. So in the future, these societies will be as vibrant as anywhere in the world. And the long divergence will be a small blip in the sands of history.
Both Pillai’s “Guns, Gods and Missionaries” and Kuran’s “Long Divergence” have been heavy, brain wracking efforts. For the next reading, we plan to read fiction. Science fiction. Two books (because I couldn’t choose, and couldn’t find a coin to flip).

“Flowers for Algernon”, by Daniel Keyes
“A fall of moondust”, by Arthur C. Clarke

Read one or read both. But come and let’s figure what science fiction is all about before we revert to our regular schedule!

(What was the first entry on the Long divergence:)
We are reading “The long divergence” by Timur Kuran. The puzzle that the book explores is why did the middle eastern countries grow so much more slowly than their western (European) counterparts. They both started at the same level in the 5th and the 6th centuries, but by the 17th/18th century, European societies were far more wealthy and more developed. Why did the industrial revolution happen in Europe rather than in the Middle East (ME). Kuran’s thesis starts from identifying Islam as the force that brought together, and kept together, the nomadic tribes of the ME, and that the source of the long divergence is the religion/the religious texts. So far as Parts I and II goes, he identifies the institutional features of Islamic partnership organisations - the waqf - as a key culprit, although these were how orgs started in Europe as well. So the ME got equal rights for all, including women, in inheritance but no long lived firms, that could readily pool diversified capital. They were in an equilibrium that they couldn’t break out of, unlike the societies in Europe. Banks appeared in European organically, and had to be imported into the ME with courts that worked along the lines of the European courts of dispute resolution. Was it because contract enforcement can not be visibly implemented in a society with “equal rights”? Was the lack of credit markets with differential interest rates a result of this, and in turn, the cause of the lack of long tenor credit contracts? By the end of Part II, Kuran seems to have fleshed out the puzzle of the Long Divergence in great detail but not really identified a credible reason. Which makes me curious about the second half. Let’s meet and discuss how he concludes on the 29th.

On 29th June, we wrapped up discussing “The long divergence” by Timur Kuran. The book’s strength lies in what it promises: why did the middle eastern countries develop slowly compared to their western counterparts, despite being richer in the 13th century. They were as smart, as interested in being rich, wanted to be more egalitarian (for example, their inheritance laws that gave equal parts of the property to all immediate family members, regardless of gender). What they were not was open to explicit dissociation with the Islamic law. When the law said corporations cannot expand from their original contributions/contributors, or that different ethnic/religious groups should have their own laws and enforcement mechanisms, this stuck as part of their culture. Kuran presents this as an absolute barrier to growth in the region. But he presents many things as equally absolute barriers to this growth. This rapidly confuses the reader because surely not everything can be an absolute barrier to growth. There is a lot of research and documentation in the book that is pitched as critical as an answer to the puzzle, but it is left to the reader to craft her own answer with little guidance of what is more important, or less. What makes this especially difficult is the repeating appearance of the same argument at different places with different references, different contexts. The book really struggles with finding it’s identity. Is it a historical narrative? Is it an economic narrative, seeking to establish a causal story? The book reads as if each of the two identities fought, won and made an appearance at different places in the book.
Perhaps an interested, sympathetic reader, should just read the last part (Conclusion). It has a summary of the features of Islamic law+the cultural preferences of the people of the Middle East that were in place at the start of the 13th century, and a summary of the three (BIG) features that Kuran is persuaded created the long divergence. But even he admits that the same was true for other regions, which didn’t end up in the same place as the Islamic countries. The puzzle is left unresolved. The book has a hopeful end about the Middle East though: that many of the features of the Middle Eastern countries/society that has been attributed to the growth gap are being replaced and adopted integrally with modern institutions. And that in the future, these societies will be as vibrant as anywhere in the world. And the long divergence will be a small blip in the sands of history.
Both Pillai’s “Guns, Gods and Missionaries” and Kuran’s “Long Divergence” have been heavy, brain wracking efforts. For the next reading, we plan to read fiction. Science fiction. Two books (because I couldn’t choose, and couldn’t find a coin to flip).

(Notes while reading the book:

Chapters/sections that resonates the most: Part III – Sections 11,12 which describes most honestly how there started a separation of dispute resolution/judicial processes for ‘non-Muslims’+‘foreigners’. The Islamic society obsessed with being illiterates who would be conned into signing something that he did not know or get cheated because he couldn’t read. So the system (a) contracted only with known parties - like the financial transactions on the BSE - (b) insisted on witness accounts in hearing cases in the Islamic courts, (c) and explicitly chose oral evidence over documents to the point that even when documents existed, oral evidence was required in the case hearings. This last part also helped the obfuscation of state legibility, which would have made it less possible for the state to protect and provide for, in that role of state. In the section titled “Islam and the documentation of contracts”, there is an account of what happened to Crete when the Ottomans took it over from the Venetians in the mid-17th century. Venetians used professional notaries to record all maritime agreements. This declined when the Ottomans took over, to the extent that even the use of receipts for money transfers became sporadic. What is sloppy is that he doesn’t follow up with what happened to maritime trade through Crete as a consequence. Instead, he sallies forth into showing that the Quran did preach the importance of documentation, and that the Islamic society chose the opposite in living their life. Kuran then goes into a long winded rant against the “capitulations” that the rulers permitted to foreigners so that they could have their cake and eat it too, and how it all backfired on them and the Islamic society in the long run. But this seems to me a story that has similar origins in the countries of the west as well, and they seemed to have come out on the better/auccesful side of history. It was not the religion. And Kuran hasn’t figured out what else it is, other than perhaps the peopls of this region being/believing that they are dominantly illiterate. We should not (continue to) make the same mistake.
In the Section titled “The absence of middle eastern consuls” (and the previous one on “Foreign privileges as facilitators of impersonal exchange”), there is the idea of associations of traders coming together to pool resources for collective bargaining. Usually to bargain with state(s). They did this to grow economies of scale from limited resources. In this, the states were supportive because they benefitted from a growth in trade. In the Middle East, long distance traders did not form associations/guilds because their states saw nothing to gain from them (on trade?).

8 Curious: for all that inheritance laws gave women equal access to the family wealth, why was there no difference in gender equality in the ME compared with the West? In fact, why did it emerge as worse?? For instance, could a woman start / manage a waqf? Kuran doesn’t seem interested in such questions.)

6th Jan 2025:
Dear all, thank you for the discussions on Monday about what we are reading and learning from “Triumph of the city: How our greatest invention makes us richer, smarter, greener, healthier and happier”. The first three chapters have been the focus of the readings so far.
The emergent narrative is that successful cities end up (a) growing wealth and (b) attracting diverse knowledge. Cities die when people who have wealth and/or knowledge leave. The examples offer lots of reasons, but this is the end consequence, in sequence – able** people leave, city dies. As long as this doesn’t happen, cities will survive, even thrive: “when a city attracts enough skilled people, some of them will be willing enough to work on the city’s problems and find solutions for even the most intractable ones”. An additional point to note: Cities can solve for problems of poverty; they cannot solve problems of social justice.
Thus far, the narrative. Let’s discuss if you disagree! :-)
For the next meeting, I propose that we read chapters 4,5,6.
So the next reading was on chapters that describe some of (a) the problems of negative externalities in cities (polluted water, cumulated waste, crime) and (b) benefits (entertainment and arts, variety of food and other such socio-cultural experiences, high fashion as a business, choices in marriage, high wages). Which leads into the who: building up vs. building out. and a discussion on skyscrapers and the anxieties that they bring into building cities. title: The Idea of India
text:
We read the “Idea of India” as a wrap up to the discussions of “The People”s Constitution’. A proposal for forthcoming readings was that we should each read out lines/paragraphs that they found most compelling, as an anchor for the discussion.
Here is one set defining Khilnani’s narrative of the idea of India.
In the beginning, “By renouncing political power, the Brahminic order created a self-coercing, self-disciplining society founded on a vision of moral order.” “This arrangement of power explains the most peculiar characteristic of India’s pre-colonial history: the perpetual instability of political rule, the constant rise and fall of dynasties and empires, combined with the society’s unusual fixity and cultural consistency. Its identity lay not in transient political authority, but in social order.”
Therefore, “..the experience, at once humiliating and enabling, of colonialism, which made it impossible for Indians to regard their own past as a sufficient resource for facing the future, and condemned them, in struggling against the subtle knots of the foreigner’s Raj, to struggle also against themselves.”
But, “If India was weakly united, it was also weakly divided: there were no politically significant regional identities that could either obstruct unification or direct it.”
“India was a society neither of liberal individuals nor of exclusive communities or nationalities, but of interconnected differences.”
And so, “Partition is the unspeakable sadness at the heart of the idea of India: a memento mori that what made India possible also profoundly diminished the integral value of the idea. It conceded something essential in the nationalist vision, the conviction that what defined India was its extraordinary capacity to accumulate and live with differences.”
Finally, “..dreams of partition and domestic purity are animated by the fantasy that all problems begin and end at the border; they do not. There is no ideological or cultural guarantee for a nation to hold together. It just depends upon human skills. That is why politics, as an arena where different projects are proposed, and decided for and against, has never been more important for Indians.”
As decided, we are now shifting into reading history, and will read “Shattered lands: Five partitions and the making of modern Asia”, by Sam Dalrymple. The plan is to read it in two parts – upto (and including) the chapter titled “The red dawn”. That will take us half way into the book.

title: Exit, Voice and Loyalty

On 21st April, we gathered to discuss “Exit, Voice and Loyalty” by A. O. Hirshman. I first read this as a 22 year old. Like all great books, reading it as a callow youth :-D and at this grand old age, meant that I learnt different things. Then, there was this great absorption of the idea of exit and voice, and how society uses it to avoid getting stuck in a rut. This time around, I saw it through the different social mechanisms of economics/markets and negotiation/politics. So the learning that I came away with was this patched up one about society climbing out of a undesirable equilibrium:
“Endogenous forces of recovery bifurcate into two contrasting, though not mutually exclusive categories of exit and voice… (Which) reflects a more fundamental schism: that between economics and politics. Exit belongs to economics, voice to politics.”
Thanks to the small and enthusiastic group who walked through the paths that I thought were old and familiar, and made neurons snap out a new idea. :-) For those of you who didn’t get through the whole lot, or weren’t able to make it to the last session, I think that I can safely say that this old book is well worth a read (and re-reads!). There was consensus on two learnings: a shocked realisation that Aden and Burma was quite an integral part of the Indian ecosystem till as late as 1935, and that everything was structurally separate by 1940. And that the separation of peoples into countries with borders was decided by two handfuls of volatile people. Perhaps it was his intention, but those painted as heros in the existing narrative come across as somewhat peevish and irrational compared to those traditionally considered scheming. But given the massive and unexpected disruption to economic and social orders, there doesn’t seem to be an obvious alternative behaviour. Some lines to remember:
“…Arakan, the diverse and densely forested region that bordered the Indian coastline. Historically, it had been an independent kingdom wedged between separate Burmese and Bangali kingdoms, resulting in an ethnic melting pot of Arakanese Buddhists, Bengali poets, Portuguese pirates, Afghan archers and even renegade ronin samurai from Nagasaki.”
“Jinnah likened politics to a game of chess – slow, methodical and pragmatic.”
“Only the Dalit leader B. R. Ambedkar commented on the irony that the same people who had argued Burma should be separated to establish “Bharat” were now crying that the “unity of India” was being broken.”
The book is easy to read (easily assimilating content, another matter!). Shall we consider wrapping this one up in a reading before year end? :-) Two proposals are (I) a solely in-person reading session on 24th December at 4:30pm, and (II) experiment with a solely online reading session on 31st December at 12noon.
There comes the decision of the next book to start in 2026! Candidates:
1. Gods, guns, and missionaries (author: Manu Pillai)
2. How China became capitalist (author: Ronald Coase and Ning Wang)
3. China’s Future (author: David Shambaugh)
4. The good communist (author: Frank N. Pieke)
Two decisions to send in your votes on!! Please email me with you choices on –
A: : (I) or (II) on the final reading of Shattered Lands, or (III) neither.
B: Which book to read next??

      Better procurement for government IT systems
      Chapter · Susan Thomas · Public finance in the digital era: Emerging themes 2026, ODI Global · Jun 2026
      Public procurementPublic financeTechnology and innovation
      
      AbstractIT systems procurement in government is no longer a back-office support function, but a critical requirement of modern state capacity. Traditional public procurement frameworks are ill-equipped for digital infrastructure. Rapid technological evolution creates an "incomplete contract" problem, rendering perfect ex-ante requirements impossible and leading to frequent change requests that trigger costly lifecycle disruptions. The continuous need for system iteration blurs the "make-or-buy" boundary, because robust internal technical expertise is needed even when development is outsourced. Building on three case-studies of public IT procurement in India, this article argues for a paradigm shift in how governments plan, procure, and maintain IT systems. It outlines an responsive framework centered on flexible contracting, early concept verification, expert-led dispute resolution, and strategic investments in state HR capabilities to successfully navigate the digital marketplace.

      Do decreases in Distance-to-Default predict rating downgrades?
      Journal article · Nidhi Aggarwal, Manish Singh, Susan Thomas · Economic Modelling 129 · Dec 2023
      Banking and creditMeasurement and dataLaw and regulation
      Working paper
      AbstractCredit rating agencies have long been criticized for being slow to downgrade ratings, when the financial health of the firm deteriorates. This stands out in sharp contrast to how security market prices of the firm respond more rapidly, during the same time.       AbstractRegulators use measures such as a fee on high order-to-trade ratio (OTR) to slow down high-frequency trading. Their impact on market quality is, however, mixed.     2023
    
      Evaluating courts from a litigant's perspective: A project report
      Working paper · Pavithra Manivannan, Geetika Palta, Susan Thomas, Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah · XKDR Forum · Dec 2023
      Courts and insolvencyMeasurement and data
      
      AbstractInformation systems about dispute resolution processes and forums that can aid litigants, a key stakeholder in the justice delivery system, are absent. We propose the development of a system that allows a litigant to comparatively evaluate the different forums where he can take his dispute for resolution. To develop this system, we first identify the types of information that can support the decision of a potential litigant on whether to take her matter to court and if yes, which court. We find that information on efficiency, effectiveness, fairness, predictability, and access to courts are crucial for a litigant's decision-making process. Subsequently, we locate data sources required to quantify such measures from the viewpoint of periodically publishing such measures in the public domain. For this purpose, the case type was narrowed down to debt disputes. We systematically collect quantifiable information about cases from the select courts' websites, namely, the Bombay High Court (Bombay HC), the Mumbai bench of the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), and the Debt Recovery Tribunal (DRT). We use data from these courts up to September 2022. We find that a litigant has the lowest chance of getting a first hearing within the first year of filing a case at the Bombay HC (37%) as compared to the NCLT or the DRT. The chance for disposal within the first year is even slimmer. There is a 1/3rd chance of disposal at the NCLT within one year of filing, while it is less than 1/5th at both the Bombay HC and the DRT. However, a case is likely to have the highest number of hearings at the NCLT. A survey questionnaire is designed and deployed to capture features of a case that cannot be quantified. We deploy the survey to capture the relative performance of each of the three courts to a sample of respondents who have litigated frequently in the courts of our interest. The results of the survey indicate that the NCLT is ranked the highest by survey participants. Bombay HC comes second, and the DRT is ranked third.

Once implemented, the law will potentially change not only the manner in which insolvency is resolved in India but also the entire credit landscape of the country.

      Better public procurement for IT in India
      Ashok Pal Singh, Karthik Suresh, Susan Thomas · XKDR Forum Working Paper 51 · Oct 2026
      Public procurementTechnology and innovation

      AbstractInformation technology (IT) systems are now ubiquitous in government. The Government of India has tripled its spending in real terms on IT procurement over the last fifteen years. IT procurement is tricky because these systems need continuous maintenance and refinement, and traditional systems of procurement are unsuitable for solving the incomplete contract problem that follows IT procurement. We build on three case studies from India – Aadhaar, Passport Seva, and MCA-21 – to make the case for why we need new thinking on IT procurement. Our solutions hinge around the fact that the government needs to build robust internal technical expertise even when system development has been outsourced. We make the case for flexible contracting, early concept verification, and strategic investments in state HR capabilities to successfully navigate the marketplace for digital services.
    
  

  
    
    
      Better methods of running subsidy programs: Evidence from the Karnataka schemes of 2023
      Jay Kulkarni, Ajay Shah, Susan Thomas · XKDR Forum Working Paper 50 · Aug 2026
      Households and inclusionPublic financeMeasurement and data
      
      AbstractGovernments in developing countries spend heavily on subsidies, yet much of the money never reaches households: the macro–micro gap. We measure this gap in Karnataka, India, across a natural experiment. Karnataka has been delivering conditional Direct Benefit Transfers (DBT) for about a decade now. In July 2023 the state introduced new “guarantee” schemes, and directed much of its DBT allocation to a near-unconditional scheme. Because administrative records are endogenous to the state that produces them, we measure household receipts independently, from the CMIE Consumer Pyramids Household Survey. We compare robust population estimates from this survey against the state’s reported expenditure on DBTs in both periods. The gap averaged about 78% over the seven pre-2023 years and fell to about 17% after the shift. The paper contributes independently measured evidence on subsidy delivery in India and a replicable method for auditing welfare programs in the presence of longitudinal data.

      AbstractIT systems procurement in government is no longer a back-office support function, but a critical requirement of modern state capacity. Traditional public procurement frameworks are ill-equipped for digital infrastructure. Rapid technological evolution creates an "incomplete contract" problem, rendering perfect ex-ante requirements impossible and leading to frequent change requests that trigger costly lifecycle disruptions. The continuous need for system iteration blurs the "make-or-buy" boundary, because robust internal technical expertise is needed even when development is outsourced. Building on three case-studies of public IT procurement in India, this article argues for a paradigm shift in how governments plan, procure, and maintain IT systems.       AbstractWe examine the impact of borrowing on consumption smoothing for households entering credit markets for the first time, using a large panel dataset with income, expenditure and financial choices of 150,000 households in India. Compared to households that never borrow, first-time borrowers are poorer, younger, less educated, and face higher income volatility. Their decision to borrow is often preceded by a change in income or consumption, regardless of whether it is a decrease or an increase. The act of borrowing increases both the level and the volatility of consumption expenditure. Credit does not help to smooth consumption, even for first time borrowers with no shocks to income and consumption. Higher volatility of consumption persists after borrowing, particularly for expenditure on non-durable goods such as food or planned household expenditure. title: Guns, Germs and Steel
text:
SCHEDULE
Session 1 (28 Sept): The Research Design & Natural Experiments
Reading: Prologue & Part 1 (Chapters 1–3)
A kickoff meeting focused on methodology and framing. It’s a light reading load, so the discussion should focus heavily on Diamond’s premise as a research proposal.
Discussion:
Deconstructing Yali’s Question (30 mins): Treat the Prologue like a problem statement in a research paper. Is “Why did human development proceed at such different rates?” a well-framed question for diagnosing modern social problems?
The Chatham Islands as a Model (45 mins): Focus intensely on Chapter 2. Have the group critique this “natural experiment.” Discuss how modern quantitative researchers isolate variables (like geography and climate) when the starting population (the Polynesians) is held constant.
The Baseline of Conquest (15 mins): Use Chapter 3 to discuss the immediate advantages of early technological disparity before diving into why those disparities existed in the next session.
Session 2 (10 Nov): Spatial Data, Density, & Systems Economics
Reading: Part 2 (Chapters 4–10) and Part 3 (Chapters 11–14)
The core analytical session. Because this covers 11 chapters, you must split the meeting into two distinct halves to prevent the conversation from becoming a disorganized sprawl.
Discussion Organization:
First Half: Geographic Determinism & Resource Economics (45 mins): Focus on Chapters 4–10. Discuss the “East-West axis” theory as a spatial data model. How do environmental baselines (domesticable plants/animals) act as the initial capital that dictates the carrying capacity of early settlements?
Second Half: Urbanization, Epidemics, & State Capacity (45 mins): Focus on Chapters 11–14. This is the most critical section for urban planners. Discuss Chapter 11 through the lens of urban epidemiology—how did early density create both innovation and catastrophic disease vectors? Transition to Chapter 14 to debate the institutional economics of centralized power, taxation, and the structural inequalities necessary to maintain complex states.
Session 3 (21 Dec): Regional Peer Review & The Science of History
Reading: Part 4 (Chapters 15–19) and Epilogue
A wrap-up and macro-level critique. The reading load is moderate, and the timing fits well with a relaxed, end-of-year review.
Discussion Organization:
Regional Case Studies (45 mins): Treat Part 4 as a series of applied literature reviews. Assign different members to briefly “present” on how well Diamond’s framework held up when applied specifically to Australia, China, the Americas, and Africa. Where does his model oversimplify regional complexities?
The Capstone Debate (45 mins): Focus on the Epilogue. Diamond argues that history and social development can be studied with the same scientific and quantitative rigor as physics or biology. Ask your group: Based on the data proxies and methodologies used in the book, did he succeed? What modern urban planning or economic datasets would you apply today to test his theories further?

title: A Fall of Moondust / Flowers for Algernon
text:
On 3rd August, we met to discuss two books of Science fiction `Flowers for Algernon, by Daniel Keyes, and A fall of moondust, by Arthur C. Clarke. Both are books written in the 1960s-1970s, when science was still at the stage of being full of promise, human beings were starry eyed about all that it promised, and science fiction was more fiction in the promises of science, and less in the realms of fantasy. Our discussions were very 21st century, when there is little to no gaps in full knowledge and awareness about science – no more starry eyes here about promises, because we are witness to where those have worked and where they haven’t. What remains though is curiosity about how society responds to science, and awareness about how human behaviour dominates in how science is used. Our debates were not on the science itself, but on whether the choices being made in these stories sat well with our individual morality. We spent our time discussing the human choices in these books: of the management teams running the moon base station, or the enterprises running the tourism and media enterprises in the “Fall of …” or the academic scientists running the experiments in “Flower for…”. Perhaps that is the greatness of both these books – both force us to confront that we accept the cold heartedness of science in delivering what we as a race need, rather than what we may want.
Back to foundational thinking about science and society in the next book to be read then! We agreed to read “Guns, germs and steel: The fates of human societies” by Jared Diamond. There are 19 chapters in this book, and given the time constraints of this last quarter of the year, let’s start with a first reading covering the Prologue and Part 1 (chapter 1–3).

On the 4 June reading, Kavya/Pavithra pointed out that JSC presents this book not as an expert in anthropology writing a story of his own making, but instead builds out of the works of others in the field, a narrative of evolution of the human race. Facts: Humanoids (Anthropocenes) existed 200,000 years ago; Agriculture was around ~ 10,000 years ago; Mad growth of the human race ~ 5,000 years ago. After dawdling for 150,000 years, how did the last 5K years of excessive surplus happen? Traditional POV: natural evolution ==> sedentism ==> agriculture and boom! The JSC-ATG argument is: 1. we (desperately) underestimate our control of fire, which enabled concertrated subsitence in smaller areas –> helps sedentism. 2. we (desperately) underestimate the costs of sticking with agriculture in one geographical region. 3. But he agrees that “How, despite its fragility, the domus of fixed-field agriculture became a hegemonic, agro-ecological and demographic bulldozer that transformed much of the world in its image, is something of a miracle.’ :-) 4. He says that there is no evidence of cause and effect but that such a system (concentrated manpower,+arable land+nutrition) had an elective affinity with political power and privilege ==> State (Boom!).
The remaining chapters are: 5. Population control: Bondage and War; 6. Fragility of the early state: Collapse as disassembly; 7. The golden age of the barbarians. Looking forward to meeting up with all reading enthusiasts to find out the rest of the story at:

Wrapped up reading “Against the grain” by James C. Scott on 9th July. Thanks to all the enthusiastic readers, constant and new.
Like the “Tyranny of experts..” and “Triump of the city..”, it challenges ideas that we take for granted about the hows and whys of the evolution of society, civilisation and the state. (1) The superpower that the human race got was fire. That set the race on this path more than the control of agriculture. (2) No state has risen without the agro-complex; agro-complexes have thrived without state (an example of Weber’s “Elective affinity”). (3) State = (walls, tax collection and officials) which means that there was a first state (Uruk in Mesopotamia) by 3200 BCE (Before Common Era). (4) The primary driver for state appeared to be collecting people, not so much as territory or physical resources. Walls were built to keep people in, more than to keep raiders out. (5) States collapse because of climate change, loss of resources, disease, war, migration, political fragility. But really, (6) the collapse of a state is merely a “loss of social complexity”. (7) Mobile peoples (“barbarians”) and sedentary populations (with/without state) should be thought of as “competitive subsistence strategies”. The narrative built in this book may come across as a bit ideological, except that these arguments are drawn from multiple sources, not all Scott’s own, covering different periods and places. He does the orchestration, but points out puzzles and the missing holes. The story of our evolution is not done yet; state is clearly new, and is IMHO the source of immense innovation. But it’s interesting that the times we are living in resonate with some of the end of times paths described in this book. What is a barbarian in the world of AI and the internet?

title: A People’s Constitution
text:
On August 6, we discussed the first two chapters (Introduction and chapter 1!) of “A people”s constitution’. It is not a difficult read, entertaining even if a tad rambling. For non-lawyers like myself, it was revealing to see a bit of the history of courts in the Introduction, and the tussle between junta and the state in Chapter 1 on the Prohibition ban. The line that clarified the puzzle for me on how there was so much conflict with the state was this: Postcolonial sovereignty is based on a contradictory logic, straddling the bureaucratic methods of colonial rule and the claim to represent a free nation. (ref: Ranabir Sammadar, “The materiality of politics: The technologies of rule”, 2007.) So much was being borrowed of the British political and judicial system, while simultaneously proclaiming full-on “independence”. Given the cruelty and immediacy of Partition, perhaps there was little chance of having strategised better. It would have been nice to be better prepared.
Next reading: the rest of the book, which is three chapters and the conclusion.

On 24 September, we wrapped up “The people”s constitution’. The book comes together in it’s Conclusion chapter. But you have to read the whole book to fully appreciate it. It is difficult to remember such a time, but at Independence “The state was being reconstituted, more than five hundred territorities were being absorbed, the administration was being rapidly expanded, and government was entering new arenas.” In debates on the constitution, we bring in the U.S. to compare. But “.. Americans had law, they made law, they inherited law, they used law and they were subject to law.” India didn’t rise from such a context. “.. many of the laws that existed until 1947 were neither made nor inherited by Indians.” It was interesting that constitutional litigation overtook civil litigation after independence. And De uses this book to demonstrate how the emergence of constitutional law as a field of bargainning between society and government benefitted those “who stood outside the consensus of what a good Indian citizen should be.” He says “The rights claims before the judiciary in the 1950s, unlike the rights claims today, were claims not for new rights but for continuing older practices that were now being challenged or forbidden by the new government. […] although a claim of cultural autonomy to protect lifestyles could be made against a colonial state, it was harder to sustain in a democratic republic. […] Despite minority rights in India having been largely understood through the realm of identity and culture, the claims made by minorities (in the 1950s) were for economic rights…. Constitutional law thus became the field in which citizens marked as deviant in the new order could recast themselves as virtuous constitutional actors.” Maybe not such a depressing book after all. :-)
Some books were suggested for the next readings (“The power broker”, “Guns… missionaries”, “Freedom and property”). Before that, let’s read “The idea of India” by Sunil Khilnani, to help to wrap up the theme of India? It is slim in size, dense in thought. Will help steel our brains to start the arduous task of reading the history books that lay ahead of us.
